paras: The lynching of John Humphreys was the killing of a Black man by masked men who broke into the county jail at Asheville, North Carolina, early on Sunday, July 15, 1888, and hanged him from a tree. Humphreys had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and the mob spent about an hour battering apart the steel cage that held him. The story ran by wire across the country, and the Charlotte Democrat called it "the first lynching known in Western North Carolina."

On July 14 a telegram from Asheville reported that Benjamin Parker's twelve-year-old daughter had been "brutally assaulted" by a Black man, and predicted that "if found he will doubtless receive little mercy from his captors." Later accounts named her Sallie Kate Parker, aged 13, and said she had been waylaid and choked in a wooded hollow on her way home from town.

About 9 o'clock on Saturday night John Humphreys was arrested "under strong suspicion." The girl had described a barefoot man in a striped shirt; Humphreys was made to change back into a striped shirt and remove his shoes, and she identified him immediately. As "whispers of lynching" spread, he was moved at 1 a.m. from the city calaboose to the steel cage of the county jail.

About 3:15 a.m., by the wire account, twenty-five to forty masked men got inside the jail before Deputy Sheriff James Worley noticed them. Worley fired on them and was answered with "a shower of bullets," though no one was reported hurt. Overpowered, he refused to give up the cage combination, so the mob tore the cage apart with sledgehammers and crowbars, took Humphreys out and hanged him from a tree about a quarter mile from the jail. Worley then rang the fire bell and led a posse in pursuit, but the mob eluded him.

The Charlotte Democrat said the posse found the body within three hundred yards of the jail, "in view of the city and the mountain side above." Several accounts repeated an unattributed rumor that Humphreys "made a full confession of his guilt before he was hanged."

No member of the mob was named, and no report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage. The Charlotte Democrat added, without a source, that "the crowd was partly made up of negroes" and that Humphreys was "a bad man from Spartanburg, S. C."

Outside the South the lynching circulated mainly as wire copy. The New York Sun ran the full account under "LYNCHED A NEGRO," and the New-York Tribune headed a shorter version "A Negro Lynched in Spite of the Sheriff." One-sentence briefs ran from Maine to California and, into August, Idaho.

Southern papers presented the hanging as deserved. The Savannah Morning News headlined it "ROPE FIXES A RAVISHER," and the Atlanta Constitution printed the Asheville dispatches under "A Season of Lynching Needed." Raleigh's State Chronicle called it "swift retribution for the most heilish of hellish crimes" and later noted that the Mt. Airy News objected only to its Sunday timing: "It is not the lynching it objects to, but the time chosen for it." Even in Sacramento, the Daily Record-Union headed its brief "A Brate [Brute] Lynched" and called Humphreys "a creature."

The one dissent came nearly four weeks later in the Charlotte Messenger, where a letter written on behalf of "the colored man" denounced "the outrageous murder of a young man of color at Asheville." The writer added, "The worst of the matter was the hanging of the wrong man, we were told," a claim no other paper repeated.

The first dispatch, sent before the arrest, gave the girl's age as twelve; later reports gave 13 and named her Sallie Kate, Sarah or Kate Parker. Most papers called the crime rape, but the State Chronicle wrote that Humphreys "attempted to rape" her. The Wilmington Daily Republican placed the lynching early Saturday, against Sunday morning in the fuller Asheville accounts; the Charlotte Democrat put the mob's arrival at 2:15 a.m., not 3:15.
On guilt, the wire accounts rested on the girl's identification and a confession rumor; the Messenger repeated hearsay that the wrong man was hanged.

reader.title: Lynching of John Humphreys
bases: A band of masked men broke into the county jail, tore apart the steel cage holding John Humphreys, an accused prisoner, and hanged him from a tree (A3, A6, A17).

Twenty-five to forty masked men overpowered the deputy in charge of the jail, took Humphreys from custody and hanged him, without any legal authority (A3, A5, A17); they acted on the accusation that he had assaulted a white girl (A3, A18).

The wire account (A3, A6) and a separate July 16 Asheville dispatch in the Charlotte Democrat (A17), with the Raleigh State Chronicle (A18), agree on the arrest, jail break and hanging; the Charlotte Messenger's doubt (A23) concerns guilt, not the killing.
